# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Review of Achterberg et al., "Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis"

This is a careful review and mostly well reported:
- The protocol was registered before the search.
- Actual hours are used where available.
- Self-rated productivity is excluded.
- Work type was coded by two independent coders (κ = 0.84).
- Per-hour and per-worker outcomes are reported side by side.
- The Discussion avoids both extremes. It rejects "sector-general" and it rejects "entirely an artifact."

The numbers are internally consistent:
- Every confidence interval is symmetric on the log scale, as it should be when pooling log ratios. For example, 13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) is 0.126 ± 0.048.
- The design and measurement counts reconcile. Twelve of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, so 6 of the 8 actual-hours studies are controlled. Nine of the 14 used manager-reported output, so 2 of the 9 controlled studies used manager-reported output.

The main problems are three overclaims (duration, bias adjustment, and "convergence") and one missing element, a formal risk-of-bias assessment.

## 1. The duration analysis does not rule out novelty effects

The claim that effects "show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" appears in the abstract as well as the Results. The analysis can't support it:

- **It compares different studies, not the same study over time.** The four long-follow-up studies are compared with the overall pool. That doesn't show whether effects *within* those studies declined. A study that started at +25% and fell to +14% would read as "no decay" here. Report early and late estimates from each long study.
- **Survivorship.** Long follow-up generally exists only where the scheme continued. Organisations that reverted, like half of Halden's retail organisations, don't produce 30-month data. Long-run studies are therefore selected for success.
- **Design mix is unknown.** If the four long studies are mostly uncontrolled with scheduled hours, the right benchmark is the uncontrolled estimate (+18.7%), not the overall 13.4%. Against that benchmark, +14.0% could even suggest decline.
- **Too imprecise.** With k = 4 and a CI of +6.2 to +22.4, substantial decay is not ruled out.

A defensible statement would be: "The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months do not show smaller effects than shorter studies, but this comparison cannot rule out novelty effects."

## 2. The per-hour outcome partly mirrors the size of the hours cut

In scheduled-hours studies, output per hour is output per worker divided by the scheduled-hours ratio. With output flat, a 10% cut produces +11% per hour and a 25% cut produces +33%. Variation in the size of the cut (inclusion requires at least 10%) therefore creates spread in per-hour effects with no change in productivity. That may account for part of the I² = 81%, and it may explain why scheduled-hours studies show larger gains than actual-hours studies.

Recommendations:
- Add the percentage reduction in hours as a moderator in the meta-regression.
- Give output per worker more prominence. It is the outcome least affected by this problem, and it carries the policy-relevant finding (−8.9% in coverage-bound work).

The reported pairs imply average reductions of about 11% to 16% across subgroups. For example, scheduled-hours studies: 0.994/1.166 ≈ 0.85. The authors should report the actual distribution of cut sizes.

## 3. The "convergence on 8 to 10%" is less independent than it sounds

The Discussion says controlled studies (8.2%), actual-hours studies (7.9%), record-based studies (9.7%) and the bias-adjusted estimate (9.1%) "converge." But:

- **The subgroups largely contain the same studies.** Most controlled studies also measure actual hours and use records. Agreement among overlapping subsets is not independent corroboration.
- **Each subgroup corrects one bias but not the others.** The controlled group includes 3 scheduled-hours studies and 2 with manager-reported output. The actual-hours group includes 2 uncontrolled studies. The Varga–Holm re-analysis showed these corrections compound. The real test is the subset that is controlled, uses actual hours *and* uses record-based output. Report that estimate, ideally split by work type, and report the 3 RCTs separately.
- **Work type is mixed in.** The controlled estimate pools discretionary and coverage-bound settings. The figure for discretionary work under the best designs is the controlled-discretionary estimate (+9.6%), and it would be more informative restricted to actual hours.

The same issue weakens the rebuttal of Varga & Holm. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups don't "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified" if each still contains studies with the other problems, and neither addresses novelty (see §1). The conclusion that the gains are not *entirely* an artifact is probably right: Varden's case-processing stratum alone supports it. But it should rest on the best-evidence subset rather than on single-feature subgroups.

## 4. The small-study adjustment is unreliable here

Trim-and-fill is known to perform poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%). Funnel asymmetry here may reflect design rather than suppressed studies: small studies are disproportionately uncontrolled pilots with scheduled hours and manager-rated output, which produce larger estimates for reasons already identified.

Recommendations:
- Run Egger's test and the funnel analysis with the design and measurement moderators included.
- Add sensitivity methods suited to heterogeneous data, such as PET-PEESE or a selection model.
- Present +9.1% as one sensitivity estimate, not as a corrected figure. Soften the publication-bias interpretation, since self-selection of organisations into pilots produces the same pattern.

## 5. No formal risk-of-bias assessment

A systematic review should assess each study with a standard tool, such as RoB 2 for the RCTs and ROBINS-I for the non-randomised studies, and summarise the certainty of evidence (e.g., GRADE). Design and measurement moderators are a partial substitute but miss specific problems like these:
- **Attrition.** Halden's withdrawals occurred after the schedule began and were mostly workload-related.
- **Contamination and spillover** in controlled studies.
- **Non-randomised controlled studies are still self-selected.** In the 6 matched or difference-in-differences studies, organisations presumably volunteered.

A PRISMA flow diagram (412 records screened down to 23 included) should also be provided.

## 6. Handling of specific studies

- **Halden.** The included figures appear to be the originally reported ones (scheduled hours, manager index, survivors only). Varga & Holm's microdata re-analysis gives corrected values for subsets. Say which version was used, and add a sensitivity analysis using the corrected values or excluding Halden.
- **Varden and other multi-stratum studies.** Varden has a discretionary stratum and a coverage-bound stratum with very different results. Was it entered once, and coded as what? Or was it entered as two strata? If strata were entered separately, the k counts and the statistical dependence between estimates need explaining. If Varden was coded "mixed," its most informative contrast is lost from the work-type analysis.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Meta-regression with k = 23.** With three correlated moderators, the 58% of variance explained is unstable. Report how much it changes when individual studies are dropped one at a time, and use the Knapp–Hartung adjustment if it wasn't used.
- **Coverage-bound consistency.** I² = 22% from 7 studies is imprecise. State whether all seven point estimates are negative; that is the stronger claim.
- **The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work may not be "real" productivity.** With fewer staff covering unchanged opening hours, each person has less idle time, so output per hour rises from fuller workloads rather than better work. Moderate the wording.
- **Sick leave (−31%).** Where the schedule removes whole days, sick days fall partly because there are fewer days on which to be absent. Adjust per scheduled day or note the issue.
- **Fatigue correlation.** The r = 0.18 is a study-level correlation across 11 studies. Note that it cannot say anything about mechanisms within individuals.

## Summary

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain is real but smaller than headline pilots | Supported |
| Gain is about 8–10% | Plausible, but needs a best-evidence subgroup estimate (controlled + actual hours + records) |
| Coverage-bound output per worker falls ~9% | Well supported; the most robust finding |
| Discretionary output per worker roughly maintained | Supported, with controlled estimates leaning slightly negative |
| Small-study bias; adjusted to +9.1% | Asymmetry is real but likely partly design-driven; the adjustment method is unreliable here |
| No decay; novelty can be set aside | Not supported |
| Not "entirely an artifact" | Probably correct, but argue it from the best-evidence subset |
| Not sector-general | Well supported |

## Suggested revisions

1. Replace the duration conclusion with within-study early-versus-late comparisons, and remove "novelty explanations can be set aside" from the abstract.
2. Add the size of the hours cut as a moderator, and give output per worker more prominence.
3. Report pooled estimates for studies that are controlled and use actual hours and records, plus the 3 RCTs separately, split by work type.
4. Add RoB 2 / ROBINS-I assessments, a GRADE summary and a PRISMA diagram.
5. Run a Halden sensitivity analysis using Varga & Holm's corrections, and explain how multi-stratum studies were handled.
6. Treat the small-study adjustment as a sensitivity analysis, adding PET-PEESE or a selection model.

With these changes, this would be the most authoritative synthesis of the evidence so far. Its central framing is right: per-hour and per-worker productivity diverge, and work type determines whether a per-hour gain makes up for the hours lost.
